title: Is the book always better?
gist: Review of Louise Willder's The Book Was Better argues that film and TV adaptations can legitimately improve on or reinterpret their source novels, citing Kubrick's The Shining, The Remains of the Day and Ishiguro's view that stories should evolve. Low market relevance; cultural commentary.

insights.claim: Around half of the 98 films that have won the Oscar for Best Picture derive from books, showing how heavily prestige cinema relies on literary source material.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Book IP is a durable feedstock for prestige film and TV; watch literary rights as a content-pipeline asset.

insights.claim: Stanley Kubrick argued that adapting a strong existing story frees a director to take creative risks while giving financial backers their best chance to recoup money and profit.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Pre-proven stories de-risk film financing, which explains studios' preference for adaptations.
insights.quote: their best chance to get their money back and hopefully make a profit

insights.claim: Books give cinema the foundations of story and a proof of concept, which is why adaptation remains a default route for studios.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Supports durable demand for literary rights and book-driven content slates.

insights.claim: The author argues that preferring the original book is partly snobbery, and that an adaptation can legitimately improve on or reinterpret its source rather than merely reproduce it.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Against the consensus 'the book was better' view; audiences may reward bolder reinterpretations.

insights.claim: Excessive reverence to the source makes an adaptation redundant, because viewers would then be better off simply reading the book.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Faithful-but-flat adaptations carry weaker differentiation and audience pull.

insights.claim: A more faithful adaptation may transfer a novel's spirit rather than film every detail, as Harold Pinter did by adding a meta story of actors filming the story in Karel Reisz's 1981 The French Lieutenant's Woman.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Spirit-over-letter is a usable test for judging adaptation quality.

insights.claim: Kazuo Ishiguro, a Nobel-winning novelist with an Oscar nomination for Best Adapted Screenplay, holds that an adaptation should move on from the original so the story grows and evolves.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Authors who welcome evolution make rights easier to license and adapt.
insights.quote: it’s when the story should grow and evolve

themes.theme: Why adaptations change: authors, censorship, medium

insights.claim: Stephen King objected that Kubrick's The Shining gave Jack Torrance no arc, yet King's own three-part TV adaptation is widely considered a dud, with 6.1 on IMDb and 54 per cent on Rotten Tomatoes versus 8.4 and 84 per cent for Kubrick's.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Author control over an adaptation does not guarantee quality or audience reception.
insights.quote: In the movie, there’s no tragedy because there’s no real change.

insights.claim: The Hays Code, in force from 1934 to 1968, shaped adaptations through self-censorship, for example softening the ending of Steinbeck's The Grapes of Wrath in John Ford's film.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Regulatory and moral constraints directly alter content; a reminder that censorship regimes reshape media output.

insights.claim: Films hold narrative advantages over novels, since soundtrack, set design, close-ups and acting can convey emotion non-verbally, as Anthony Hopkins does in the 1993 Remains of the Day.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Medium-specific strengths explain why some adaptations outperform text originals.

insights.claim: Virginia Woolf's 1926 essay 'The Cinema' criticised film for lacking the depth of the novel, representing the classic case against adaptation.
insights.speaker: Daniel Rey
insights.so_what: Historical context for the long-running page-versus-screen debate.
insights.quote: A kiss is love. A broken cup is jealousy.
